title: Neonatal resuscitation at birth
subject: paediatrics
setting: Labour room, operation theatre, SNCU, NICU
summary: Keep the baby warm, dry and stimulate, and start effective ventilation within the golden minute; start 3:1 chest compressions only if heart rate stays below 60/min after 30 seconds of ventilation that moves the chest, then give IV adrenaline 0.01 to 0.03 mg/kg (AHA/AAP 2025).

sections.title: Prepare and assess at birth
items: Every birth needs a trained person with a checked bag and mask, suction, warmer and timer. Brief the team and assign roles when risk factors are present (preterm, meconium-stained liquor, fetal distress, multiple birth, maternal infection).
Ask at birth: term gestation, good tone, breathing or crying? If yes, keep skin-to-skin with the mother, dry and cover, and continue routine care with monitoring of breathing and temperature.

Babies not needing resuscitation (term and preterm): defer cord clamping for at least 60 seconds. Non-vigorous babies of 35 weeks or more: intact cord milking may be reasonable. Never milk the cord below 28 weeks.

Assess heart rate first by auscultation (count for 6 seconds and multiply by 10). Once ventilation is needed, add a pulse oximeter on the right hand or wrist (preductal) and ECG leads; ECG is the fastest and most accurate heart rate monitor.

sections.title: Golden minute: initial steps and ventilation
items: Receive in warm dry linen, dry thoroughly, remove wet linen, position the head neutral or slightly extended and stimulate by rubbing the back. Suction mouth then nose only if the airway looks obstructed.

Do not routinely suction the mouth, nose or trachea, including babies born through meconium-stained liquor, whether vigorous or not. Intubate and suction the trachea only if it is obstructed during ventilation.

Start ventilation within 60 seconds of birth if apnoeic, gasping or heart rate below 100/min despite initial steps: 30 to 60 breaths/min (NSSK teaches 40 to 60/min), initial peak pressure 20 to 30 cmH2O, adjusted to gentle visible chest rise.

Starting oxygen: air (21%) at 35 weeks or more; 21 to 30% at 32 to 34+6 weeks; 30 to 100% below 32 weeks. Titrate to the preductal SpO2 targets. Start with room air where oxygen is not available; do not delay ventilation.

A rising heart rate is the main sign of effective ventilation. If the chest does not rise, take corrective steps (mask seal, reposition, suction, open mouth, increase pressure) and consider a laryngeal mask (34 weeks or more) or endotracheal tube.
Preterm babies breathing spontaneously with respiratory distress or hypoxia: give CPAP rather than routine intubation.

sections.title: Chest compressions, adrenaline and volume
items: Start chest compressions if heart rate remains below 60/min after 30 seconds of ventilation that moves the chest, preferably through an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask. Increase oxygen to 100% during compressions.

Use the 2-thumb encircling technique on the lower third of the sternum, depth one-third of the chest diameter, 3 compressions to 1 breath (90 compressions and 30 breaths per minute). Reassess heart rate after 60 seconds.

If heart rate is still below 60/min after 60 seconds of compressions with adequate ventilation, give adrenaline (epinephrine) 0.01 to 0.03 mg/kg IV (0.1 to 0.3 mL/kg of 0.1 mg/mL), preferably by umbilical venous catheter (IO if UVC not possible). Repeat every 3 to 5 minutes.

While access is being obtained, endotracheal adrenaline 0.05 to 0.1 mg/kg (0.5 to 1 mL/kg of 0.1 mg/mL) may be given. If the response is inadequate, give IV adrenaline as soon as access is obtained, regardless of the interval.

Known or suspected blood loss (pallor, poor perfusion, abruption, cord accident) with no response to adrenaline: 0.9% saline or O Rh-negative blood 10 to 20 mL/kg IV over 5 to 10 minutes, repeated if the response is inadequate.
Stop compressions once heart rate is 60/min or more. Stop ventilation once breathing is effective and heart rate is above 100/min, then wean oxygen to the saturation targets.

sections.title: Targets and monitoring
items: Preductal SpO2 targets after birth: 1 min 60 to 65%, 2 min 65 to 70%, 3 min 70 to 75%, 4 min 75 to 80%, 5 min 80 to 85%, 10 min 85 to 95%. Avoid hyperoxia; wean oxygen as saturation rises.

Keep temperature 36.5 to 37.5 °C from birth to admission; prevent hypothermia (below 36 °C) and hyperthermia (above 38 °C). Below 32 weeks use a plastic bag or wrap, a hat, radiant warmer and a warm delivery room.

After prolonged ventilation or advanced resuscitation (intubation, compressions, adrenaline), monitor breathing, heart rate, SpO2, temperature and blood glucose early and until stable. Rewarm babies who are unintentionally below 36 °C.

sections.title: After resuscitation
items: Babies who needed more than brief ventilation, or any compressions or adrenaline, need admission to an SNCU or NICU. Continue ventilation without interruption during transfer.
Babies of 36 weeks or more with moderate to severe hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy: offer therapeutic hypothermia started within 6 hours (core 33.5 °C for 72 hours) under a defined protocol.
In India, after the HELIX trial, cool only highly selected infants in level III/IV NICUs with servo-controlled equipment and 1:1 nursing; never cool babies below 35 weeks.
Avoid passive cooling or rewarming without core temperature monitoring, including during transport.

sections.title: Withholding and stopping resuscitation
items: If there is no detectable heart rate after all steps (effective ventilation, compressions, adrenaline and volume), discuss stopping with the team and family at around 20 minutes after birth.
Not starting and stopping life-sustaining treatment are ethically equivalent. For conditions likely to cause early death or severe morbidity, agree a plan with the family before birth where possible.
When resuscitation is withheld or stopped, keep the baby warm and comfortable, allow the family to hold the baby, and document the discussion.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Moving to compressions or drugs before ventilation is effective: most bradycardic newborns respond to good ventilation alone.
Routine 100% oxygen in term babies, or not titrating oxygen once pulse oximetry is available.
Letting the baby get cold during resuscitation, especially preterm babies; hypothermia increases mortality.
Delaying ventilation to suction meconium or to wait for oxygen or intubation.

drugs.name: Adrenaline (epinephrine) 0.1 mg/mL (1 mg in 10 mL)
drugs.dose: 0.01 to 0.03 mg/kg (0.1 to 0.3 mL/kg) IV or IO, repeat every 3 to 5 minutes while heart rate is below 60/min
drugs.notes: Endotracheal 0.05 to 0.1 mg/kg (0.5 to 1 mL/kg) only while IV access is obtained. Follow IV doses with a saline flush.

drugs.name: 0.9% sodium chloride (volume expansion)
drugs.dose: 10 to 20 mL/kg IV or IO over 5 to 10 minutes, repeat if response is inadequate
drugs.notes: Known or suspected blood loss. Use O Rh-negative blood if loss is substantial.

drugs.name: Oxygen
drugs.dose: Start 21% at 35 weeks or more, 21 to 30% at 32 to 34+6 weeks, 30 to 100% below 32 weeks; 100% during chest compressions
drugs.notes: Titrate to preductal SpO2 targets by minute of life.
